title: Giving the exchange: name what you get back
outcomes: Says what an exchange sacrifice costs on the usual count and why that count is only a rule of thumb
Names the reason for a given exchange sacrifice (here a passed pawn or a broken king shelter) and its payoff
Tests whether a minor piece can challenge the gain before giving the exchange
Says "no sacrifice here" when nothing lasting is on offer

steps.text: The counting values 1, 3, 3, 5, 9 are a **rule of thumb**: a rook for a minor piece costs about two units of material. It is a **sacrifice** only if you can name what you get that lasts: a passed pawn that cannot be stopped, a broken king shelter, a minor piece that dominates, or a blockade. "It looks active" is not a reason. No named gain: keep the rook.

steps.caption: White to move. The exchange sacrifice, step by step.

line.say: The rook takes the bishop. Cost: about two points on the usual count.
The pawn takes back. Now no black pawn stands in front of the a-pawn.
The a-pawn runs. The tablebase confirms that White wins.

claims.statement: After Rxc6 bxc6 the a-pawn is a passed pawn.

steps.text: **The gain has to last.** Before giving the exchange, ask what the opponent can do about the gain: can a minor piece come to meet the pawn, or take what you win? In the next exercise one knight moves and the same sacrifice fails. Only the passed pawn and the broken shelter are tested here: a dominating piece and a blockade are described but not tested.

steps.title: The same sacrifice, one piece moved
steps.prompt: In the first position Rxc6 bxc6 wins. Now the black knight stands elsewhere. Predict, then check.

steps.text: No labels now. In each position ask what a move would gain and whether that gain lasts. Some positions have a winning move and some do not. The next three exercises are silent.

steps.prompt: For the last sacrifice you found, write the reason in one line, and the move or piece that could have spoiled it. If you cannot name both, the sacrifice is not ready.
